performers: Skidmore College Orchestra, per the Free Music Archive and Internet Archive; not named on the Commons page
question: How does a short piece make quarrelling children sound like a tune?
intro: Children squabble in a Paris garden after their games. The minute-long picture is a small three-part scherzo; listen for the chatter that frames a smoother, more singing middle. Instruments named here follow Ravel’s orchestration, the probable but undocumented version.

sections.label: The chatter returns
sections.mNote: opening figures return, ending with understatement

cues.title: Woodwind chatter, plucked strings
cues.text: Bustling woodwinds are punctuated by pizzicato strings. The opening is busy but quiet: about five detected attacks a second, at a modest level near −22 dB, so the quarrel is heard from a little way off.
cues.evidence: Onsets per second are 5.0, 4.2 and 4.8 at 0:00, 0:05 and 0:10; relative level is −22.8 to −20.7 dB. Woodwinds and pizzicato strings: Philharmonia guide (Joanna Wyld).

cues.title: A lost picture and a children’s song
cues.text: Hartmann’s Tuileries picture is lost, and the children in it were probably added for scale. Mussorgsky had already dedicated a children’s song to him: “In the Corner”, the second of The Nursery, in 1870.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s Pictures at an Exhibition article: the Tuileries picture is lost and its figures likely added for scale (movement 3), and the 1870 dedication of “In the Corner” to Hartmann (composition history). Related edge: hartmann-pictures--mussorgsky-pictures-1874.

cues.title: Chatter again, then a shrug
cues.text: The opening ideas return around 0:48 after a build to the loudest windows, 0:45–0:50. The picture ends quietly, with a witty understatement; the final window sits at −24 dB.
cues.evidence: Boundary at 0:48 (novelty 0.81); relative level −12.8 dB (0:45), −13.9 (0:50), −22.1 (0:55), −24.4 (1:00); onsets per second 4.0 at 0:55. The witty understated ending: Philharmonia guide.

transitions.title: Chatter thins into a singing line
transitions.how: The woodwind chatter quietens and the number of attacks drops sharply. A smoother violin theme, still animated, rises higher in register, so the colour brightens even though the level stays low. The ear moves from a texture of short figures to one long line: the same quick pulse continues, but it is now carried by one sustained voice.
transitions.evidence: Boundaries at 0:22 and 0:28 (novelty 0.78, 0.79); onsets per second 4.2 (0:05) to 0.8 (0:30); brightness 1,197 Hz (0:25) to 1,488 Hz (0:35). The violin theme is from the Philharmonia guide; the pulse continuing under it is an inference from the score’s metre.

transitions.title: A build brings the opening back
transitions.how: The violin theme builds towards the loudest windows of the picture, 0:45 to 0:50, and the opening chatter returns. After a quick climax the level drops about nine decibels by 0:55 and the picture ends on a quiet, witty understatement, not a loud cadence. The quarrel simply stops, as children’s quarrels do.
transitions.evidence: Boundary at 0:48 (novelty 0.81); relative level −20.7 dB (0:35), −12.8 dB (0:45), −13.9 dB (0:50), −22.1 dB (0:55), −24.4 dB (1:00); onsets per second 4.0 at 0:55. The returning opening ideas and understated ending are from the Philharmonia guide and the score’s ternary form; the report cannot time individual figures.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Skidmore College Orchestra (orchestra, as stated by the Free Music Archive; conductor unknown)
fields.note: The Commons page names no performer (“see Musopen for performance author information”). The Free Music Archive album of 15 tracks by the Skidmore College Orchestra lists a track of the same title and length (1:03; this file is 1:02), and the Internet Archive item for the first Promenade credits the same orchestra. The identification of this file with that track rests on title and length; the Musopen performer page was not opened. Conductor: unknown.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Orchestral performance; Ravel’s 1922 orchestration is the probable version but is not named by any source
fields.note: Neither Commons, the Free Music Archive nor the Internet Archive names the orchestrator. The album’s four Promenades (none between “Samuel Goldenberg and Schmuÿle” and Limoges) match Ravel’s layout, and a 2015 Commons talk-page comment calls the recording Ravel’s orchestration of a rather poor Skidmore performance. The commenter gives no source. Instrument names in the listening notes follow Ravel’s scoring conditionally, as the introduction says; the audio report does not identify instruments.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: No session date is documented. The Internet Archive item says “date unknown, 2008 at the latest”; the Free Music Archive lists the album as released 6 April 2009; this file was uploaded to Commons on 2008-01-21. None of these is a recording date.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: No venue is documented. The Free Music Archive biography describes the orchestra as a semi-professional ensemble of Skidmore students and regional professionals; this is not a recording location.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Mussorgsky’s piano suite (he died in 1881) is public domain; Commons marks the music PD-old-100. An orchestration is a separate work with its own term and is not cleared here.
fields.note: The Commons notice covers Mussorgsky’s music only. If the version is Ravel’s, his orchestration is not assessed in this dossier.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 1 — recording release: PD-author public-domain dedication by Musopen, with Wikimedia VRTS permission ticket 2008012110017088.
fields.note: The file description applies PD-author|Musopen to the recording separately from PD-old-100 for the music, and cites the VRTS ticket; the page is in “Items with VRTS permission confirmed”. Musopen’s reproduced policy says the music is public domain with no restrictions; its requests not to sell the recordings and to credit Musopen are courtesy requests, not a non-commercial licence. The Internet Archive copy of the first Promenade is marked CC0 1.0. Session date is not needed for this route.

composer.epithet: He made Russian speech, public crowds and the noises of ordinary life determine the shape of opera.
facts: Piano with Anton Gerke; composition informally with Mily Balakirev; no conservatory education
Guards officer until 1858; civil servant, including work in the Forestry Department
Balakirev, Borodin, Cui and Rimsky-Korsakov; the critic Vladimir Stasov
Operas, dramatic songs and piano music; many works unfinished or published in other composers’ revisions
composer.background:
Mussorgsky grew up on his family’s estate at Karevo, where his mother taught him the piano and his nurse supplied stories that he later associated with his earliest improvisations. The household belonged to the landowning class. The peasant voices he eventually put into songs and operas came from another social world. Sent to Saint Petersburg for schooling, he studied piano with Anton Gerke and entered the School of Guards Cadets in 1852. In 1856 he joined the Preobrazhensky Regiment. His first published piano piece, a polka, belonged to the drawing room.

Meeting Dargomyzhsky and then Balakirev redirected that education. Balakirev taught through playing, criticism and the examination of scores. Mussorgsky left the army in 1858, but composing did not provide a living. The emancipation of the serfs in 1861 disrupted the estate income on which his family depended, and he eventually took civil-service posts. The group later called the Five brought together different professions and musical methods: Borodin was a chemist, Cui a military engineer, Rimsky-Korsakov a naval officer. Their shared opposition to imported academic authority concealed substantial musical disagreements.
